For three decades, from the 1980s to the 2010s, speech recognizers were built from hidden Markov models. Their components are still visible in today’s systems: the MFCC or mel features, the 10 ms frames, the phonemes as units, the language model, and the search for the most probable transcript. We first state the problem, then build the recognizer from the phoneme upward, look at how it copes with speaking rate, speakers, and microphones, and finally follow its replacement by neural networks.

children.value: The acoustic model is trained on transcribed speech, the language model on text alone, of which far more exists. The language model resolves what the sound leaves open: “recognize speech” and “wreck a nice beach” sound almost the same, and the language model prefers the first.
The observations are the MFCC vectors of

: 13 coefficients from frames of 25 ms with a hop of 10 ms, extended by their first and second differences over time to 39 values. MFCCs describe the spectral envelope, the resonances of the vocal tract that distinguish one sound from another, and discard the fine structure of the harmonics. The features therefore depend little on the pitch of the speaker, which carries intonation but not the phoneme in most languages. They do not remove noise, and they do not compensate for the speaking rate; the model has to handle both.

children.value: finds the most probable path through the composite HMM with the Viterbi algorithm of
, which yields the phonemes, the words, and their time stamps at once. The composite HMM has millions of states, so decoders keep only the paths whose score lies within a

In practice, the language model score is also raised to a power, a scale factor tuned on held-out data, because the acoustic probabilities of 100 frames per second overwhelm the few word probabilities otherwise.
Training needs no time alignment. Each training utterance comes with its transcript, the dictionary turns the transcript into a chain of phoneme HMMs, and the Baum-Welch algorithm of

estimates where each phoneme starts and ends while it estimates the parameters. The dictionary also sets the limit of the vocabulary: a word that is not in it cannot be recognized at all, which hits names, new terms, and words from other languages, exactly the words that searches often contain.

Hinton et al. (2012) summarized the results of four research groups, in which such networks outperformed Gaussian mixtures on a variety of benchmarks, sometimes by a large margin. Within a few years, hybrid systems had replaced Gaussian mixtures in most recognizers.
The next step removed the HMM and the alignment.
(CTC, Graves et al., 2006) trains a recurrent network (
) to output one symbol per frame, letters or phonemes, plus a

symbol for “nothing new”. A frame sequence maps to a label sequence by merging repeated symbols and then deleting the blanks: “h h _ e l l _ l o” becomes “hello”, where the blank between the two l’s keeps them apart. The training objective sums the probabilities of all frame sequences that map to the transcript, with a forward-backward recursion like that of
. No phoneme boundaries are needed, and a network that outputs letters needs no pronunciation dictionary.
) finally map the whole spectrogram to a sequence of text tokens. Whisper, described in

, is the prominent example. It produces subword tokens, so it can write words that no dictionary listed, although it may misspell a rare name. The elements of the classical pipeline remain inside: log mel features with 10 ms hops, and a decoder that acts as a language model.
Once speech is text, it enters the inverted index of

like any document, with time stamps that let a search jump to the moment a word was spoken. Recognition errors become retrieval errors, however: a word that was misrecognized cannot be found, and a word that was inserted produces false matches. Systems mitigate this by indexing alternatives, such as the several best transcripts or a lattice of competing words with their probabilities, so that a query can match a word that was not the top choice.
skips the words. It indexes the recognized phoneme sequence with overlapping

, translates the query into phonemes with the pronunciation dictionary or a grapheme-to-phoneme model, and ranks passages by the n-grams they share with the query. This finds words that the vocabulary did not contain, and it tolerates partial errors. A query for “Basel” /b ɑː z ə l/ and a transcript that heard “basil” /b æ z ə l/ share one of three phoneme trigrams and two of four bigrams, while the two words share nothing.
